articleTitle: Operational needs for electronic displays at sea
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electronic Displays for Use at Sea (Digest No. 1997/027)
abstract: Some examples are given of electronic displays which might be found on board a ship. Their uses and operational aspects are examined. Emphasis is placed on electronic chart systems and the needs of the Master.

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electronic Displays for Use at Sea (Digest No. 1997/027)
abstract: The recent issue of the Back-up Requirements for ECDIS (Electronic Chart Display and Information Systems) by IMO (International Maritime Organization) is an important step in the global adoption of electronic charts as a legal alternative to the paper chart. This paper has outlined the advantages and disadvantages of some of the suggested arrangements for back-up and has attempted to identify which solutions will meet the new IMO requirements. Over a period of some years we can expect some convergence in the specific solutions that are used for back-up, particularly in the context of integrated bridges for newly built vessels. These are likely to include the use of a second ECDIS or a chart radar, probably through the concept of multi-function displays. Vessels retro-fitted with ECDIS are likely to see more diverse back-up arrangements. Whilst much emphasis has been put on the equipment standards for back-up it is essential that the mariner is properly trained in preparing for and coping with ECDIS failure.

articleTitle: Future developments in integrated bridge control systems
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electronic Displays for Use at Sea (Digest No. 1997/027)
abstract: In an integrated control network, all relevant ship systems are integrated into a single ship wide data network. By means of this network, there is a direct communication path between any two components connected by the control system. In addition the number of components added into the network is irrelevant and theoretically should allow equipment types to be changed easily. An integrated control network must comply with IMO and class requirements and in fact some aspects require additional treatment because of these requirements, namely alarm handling and essential control functions which require redundancy and continuous handling from the network.

articleTitle: Electronic chart displays for use in VTMIS
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electronic Displays for Use at Sea (Digest No. 1997/027)
abstract: The origins of the Electronic Chart Display and Information Systems (ECDIS) lie in the twin needs for efficient transfer of data within and between Hydrographic Offices and the more efficient use of hydrographic data by the main end users-ships at sea. However, as with many other developments in technology, it is now apparent that the combination of digital chart data with modern computer and communication applications can improve performance in several maritime areas. For many the logical choice for this digital chart data is that required for ECDIS, with all the benefits of agreed international standards and Hydrographic Office quality that this implies; in fact, for Vessel Traffic Services (VTS), the use of ECDIS as the Geographic Information System (GIS) has already been recommended. One of the benefits which the new technology brings is the ability for better informed supervision of remote activities at a price which companies, organisations and authorities are prepared to contemplate. This subject is explored with special reference to VTMIS (Vessel Traffic Management Information Systems) its practical limitations.

articleTitle: Displays for use in coastal waters
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electronic Displays for Use at Sea (Digest No. 1997/027)
abstract: This paper describes work done to develop an intelligent decision support system and associated display for marine pilots. This system is based around the concept of an electronic chart with DGPS positioning and provides real time advice to pilots and ships masters in confined port approach areas. The system is intended to demonstrate how advanced Electronic Chart equipment can provide added value to ship safety in restricted waters. The questions that had to be resolved in developing an interface to such a system may provide some stimulus to those involved in the design of coastal navigation systems.

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electronic Displays for Use at Sea (Digest No. 1997/027)
abstract: Electronic displays fitted on the bridges of ships have become more accurate, and are generally much easier to operate and to read than they used to be, but there is still scope for improvement in the specification, the design and the installation of these systems before they can be truly said to provide their full potential for assisting in the safe and speedy navigation of ships. The author has worked as a ship's Deep Sea Pilot; this involves boarding ships, usually at the western end of the English Channel and then piloting these ships between various ports in northern Europe. The ships are mostly fast container ships, or car carriers, or medium to large bulk carriers and tankers. Experience gained on board, about the good and the less good points about the different electronics systems and displays that they are fitted with, is outlined.

articleTitle: Displays for future air navigation systems
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electronic Displays for Use at Sea (Digest No. 1997/027)
abstract: This paper discusses the current displays and traffic control of commercially operated aircraft and discusses the currently planned changes with new systems to handle the predicted increases in traffic. Although no discussion of maritime traffic control systems is included, it is hoped that the approaches and problems described may have some relevance. Aircraft display systems will change significantly due to required changes in air traffic control systems. The progressive increase in airspace congestion will lead to a position where the current, manually controlled, air traffic control system will no longer be able to cope. Some capacity increase may be achieved by partial automation of the air traffic control system enabling a reduction in air traffic controller to pilot conversation. New navigation technology utilising Global Positioning System can provide more accurate navigation which would allow relaxation of the current tightly defined aircraft routes delimited by Navaid positions to a free flight environment where aircraft routes are not defined. Changes are constrained by the mandatory requirement to maintain and preferably improve the overall safety of the system.

articleTitle: Development in display technology [for naval ship command and control systems]
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Electronic Displays for Use at Sea (Digest No. 1997/027)
abstract: Ultra Electronics Limited is a market-led group of businesses specialising in advanced technology solutions for niche aerospace and defence markets globally. Through the Command and Control Systems Division Ultra Electronics has been involved in the design, manufacture and support of Naval Command Systems, Fire Control and Weapon Interfacing Systems. The current range of equipment is being fitted in the RN carriers, destroyers, frigates and submarines as well as by overseas navies. A range of new workstation products is being developed, offering maximum flexibility. These products utilise an open architecture and have a wide range of standard processing interface options. The use of the latest flat panel display technology offers significant advantages to these new products and systems.
